pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Conductors and insulators

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS2 Year 4 Electricity, statutory):** 'recognise some common conductors and insulators, and associate metals with being good conductors.'

- **Standards — US National (NGSS):** no direct grade-3/4 performance expectation; energy/current strand 4-PS3-2 foreshadowed only. UK-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Children find out which materials let electricity through (conductors) and which do not (insulators) by testing them in the gap of a circuit, and learn that most metals are good conductors. The reasoning is empirical: put the material in the loop, does the lamp light? The topic also reinforces the complete-loop rule — an insulator in the gap is just another kind of break.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 8-9).
bestPractices: Use a test-circuit with a gap (two crocodile clips): drop a material across the gap and the lamp lights for conductors, stays dark for insulators — the circuit IS the test instrument.
Run predict-then-test-then-record: children predict each material, test it, and log conductor/insulator in a table; the prediction surfaces their ideas and the result corrects them.

Test a wide, deliberately varied set — several metals (steel, copper, aluminium, a coin), plus wood, plastic, rubber, glass, paper, fabric, and water/graphite as talking points — so the metals→conductor generalisation emerges from evidence, not assertion.
Connect to real life: explain why wires have a metal core (conductor) and a plastic coating (insulator) — the plastic keeps the electricity in the metal and us safe.

Keep the claim calibrated: 'most metals are good conductors' and 'most non-metals are insulators' — avoid overgeneralising, and note interesting exceptions (graphite conducts; pure water barely does) as enrichment, not core.
keyRepresentations: A gap-in-the-loop test rig with two crocodile clips and a bulb — the canonical conductor/insulator tester.
A predict-test-record results table: material | prediction | conductor or insulator.
A two-column sort: conductors (metals highlighted) vs insulators (wood, plastic, rubber, glass).
A cutaway of an electrical wire: metal core (conductor) inside a plastic sheath (insulator).
commonMisconceptions: 'All metals are magnetic / all shiny things conduct' — conflating conduction with magnetism or shininess; the test, not appearance, decides (a shiny painted surface may not conduct).
Thinking the plastic-coated wire conducts along its plastic, or not realising the metal inside is the conductor and the plastic the insulator.
Believing an insulator in the gap 'slows' the electricity rather than stopping the loop entirely — at this level it simply doesn't light.
Overgeneralising from one metal or assuming non-metals never conduct (graphite/pencil lead is a useful counter-case).
Thinking thickness or size of the object determines conduction rather than the material it is made of.

learn.summary: Children aged 8–9 learn to distinguish conductors (materials that let electricity flow) from insulators (materials that block it), and to generalise that most metals are good conductors while most non-metals are insulators. The core method is empirical: place a material in the gap of a simple circuit and see whether the bulb lights. The curriculum frames this as a hands-on enquiry; the primary activity is a predict–test–record investigation with a real materials kit, with on-screen or interactive-image work as useful companions for prediction, varied material sets, instant recording, and fixing vocabulary.

activities.title: Predict–test–record with a gapped circuit
feedback: When a copper strip or steel paperclip lights the bulb and a wooden lolly stick or rubber band leaves it dark, point out the result went into the correct column.
If a prediction is wrong, treat it as useful: the test corrected the idea — ask what surprised them and why.
Once the table is full, ask the child to read off which column the metals landed in, so the generalisation comes from their recorded data.
A loose clip or a tarnished surface can give an unexpected 'no light' — check the contact and retest so results reflect the material, not the connection.
activities.rationale: The UK Year 4 statutory requirement is to recognise common conductors and insulators and associate metals with being good conductors; a predict–test–record cycle across a varied material set builds the generalisation from evidence and surfaces then corrects children's prior ideas.
sourceClaims: Year 4 statutory requirement: recognise common conductors and insulators, and associate metals with being good conductors.
Children conflate conduction with shininess/magnetism and misunderstand plastic-coated wire; predict-test-record across a varied material set builds the metals→conductor generalisation from evidence.
learnerActions: Set up (or use) a test circuit with a battery, bulb and a gap bridged by two crocodile clips, so the circuit itself is the test instrument.
For each material, first write a prediction: 'Will the bulb light? Conductor or insulator?' before testing.
Drop or clip the material across the gap, observe whether the bulb lights, and log the result in a table with columns: material | prediction | result (conductor/insulator).
Test a deliberately wide, varied set: several metals (steel paperclip, copper strip, aluminium, a coin), plus wood (lolly stick), plastic (ruler), rubber band, glass, paper, and fabric.
After testing, step back and look at the filled table: notice that the conductor column has filled with metals while wood, plastic, rubber and glass sit in the insulator column.
State the pattern you discovered in your own words, e.g. 'metals are the good conductors'.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether a material conducts is decided by what it is made of, not how it looks. Testing a varied set lets the 'metals are good conductors' generalisation emerge from the child's own evidence rather than being asserted.

activities.title: Surprise cards: testing the rule's edges
feedback: When the dull metal lights the bulb and the shiny plastic (or painted tab) stays dark, ask what that shows about the 'shiny things carry electricity' rule.
If the dull metal fails to light, check whether the clip is sitting on a tarnished or painted patch rather than bare metal, and retest on a clean spot.
If a child classifies hard wood or glass as a conductor, have them test both and sort by 'is it actually a metal?' instead of 'is it hard?'.
Present graphite conducting and water barely conducting as enrichment that refines the rule, not as material to memorise.
activities.rationale: Children commonly conflate conduction with shininess, magnetism, or hardness; deliberately chosen counter-cases (dull metal vs shiny plastic or painted metal, graphite, hard insulators) confront these cues with evidence and keep the generalisation calibrated.
sourceClaims: Children conflate conduction with shininess/magnetism and misunderstand plastic-coated wire; predict-test-record across a varied material set builds the metals→conductor generalisation from evidence.
learnerActions: Predict and then test a dull or unpolished metal object (making sure the clip touches bare metal, not a tarnished patch) against a shiny object that does not conduct at its surface — for example a shiny plastic object (a non-metal), or a painted metal tab where the clips touch only the paint, which insulates so the bulb stays dark even though the tab is metal underneath — saying which you think will light the bulb AND why before testing.

Test a pencil-lead / graphite rod as a 'huh?' case: graphite is a non-metal that conducts. A thin pencil lead also contains clay and is a poorer conductor than metal, so a filament bulb may glow only dimly or not visibly. A short, thick graphite rod, or an LED or buzzer in place of the bulb, shows the effect more reliably.
Compare hard glass and hard wood (both insulators) with a softer metal, to check whether hardness decides conduction.
Discuss as enrichment: graphite conducts, and pure water barely conducts — these are interesting exceptions, not the core rule.
activities.intendedInsight: Surface cues like shininess and hardness do not decide conduction: a dull metal still conducts (where the clip reaches bare metal), while a shiny plastic or a painted-over metal still blocks current at its surface. 'Most metals conduct' and 'most non-metals insulate' is the calibrated claim, with a few noted exceptions.

activities.title: Why wires are made the way they are
feedback: If a child says the plastic coating carries the electricity, point to the metal inside as the conductor and the plastic as insulation and protection.
If a child says an insulator 'slows' the current, clarify that at this level it simply breaks the loop and the bulb does not light.
activities.rationale: Connecting the classification to the everyday wire gives a real-world anchor for the conductor/insulator distinction and addresses the common misconception that the plastic sheath conducts.
sourceClaims: Children conflate conduction with shininess/magnetism and misunderstand plastic-coated wire; predict-test-record across a varied material set builds the metals→conductor generalisation from evidence.
learnerActions: Examine (or view a cutaway of) an electrical wire: identify the metal core and the plastic sheath.
Explain which part conducts (the metal core) and which part insulates and keeps us safe (the plastic coating).
Connect to the loop rule: an insulator placed in the gap is just another kind of break, so the bulb simply does not light.
activities.intendedInsight: A wire deliberately combines a conductor (metal core to carry the electricity) and an insulator (plastic sheath to keep the electricity contained and us safe). An insulator in the circuit gap stops the loop rather than slowing the electricity.

activities.title: Sort and check (classification practice)
feedback: For a correct sort, confirm the reasoning ('it's a metal, so it conducts') rather than only the answer.
For an error, route back to a test: predict, place it in the gap, and observe.
A sort can check and reinforce classification, but it does not itself run the physical test or elicit the child's own reasoning — use it after hands-on investigation.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and selection tasks map directly onto the learning outcome and assess the metals generalisation. They test and consolidate classification rather than build the investigative reasoning, so they work best after hands-on testing.
learnerActions: Sort a set of materials into two groups: conductors and insulators, with metals highlighted as a cue.
Answer 'which of these would make the bulb light?' selection questions and match materials to their category.
For any unfamiliar material, describe how you would turn it into a fair test for conduction (place it in the circuit gap, keep the rest of the circuit the same, see if the bulb lights).
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate and check the conductor/insulator vocabulary and the metals generalisation, and recognise that a fair circuit test — not appearance — settles uncertain cases.

constraints: The standard is an enquiry to be performed: a real materials-testing kit (battery–bulb circuit with crocodile-clip leads, a tray of everyday materials, and a results sheet) gives tactile experience and authentic measurement uncertainty (a loose clip, a tarnished surface) that a clean simulation smooths away. Treat on-screen benches as companions, not replacements, for the physical investigation.

An interactive-image / tap-to-reveal chart or labelled wire cutaway can deliver the facts and fix vocabulary cleanly but does not run the child's own predict–test investigation; use it to support, not substitute, the enquiry.
Sorting and selection tasks assess and consolidate classification; they check rather than build investigative reasoning and should follow hands-on testing.

Keep claims calibrated: say 'most metals are good conductors' and 'most non-metals are insulators'. Treat graphite (conducts) and pure water (barely conducts) as enrichment exceptions, not as core rules to memorise.
At this level, present an insulator in the gap as breaking the loop (bulb does not light), not as 'slowing' the electricity.

Conductor/insulator results depend on genuine metal contact: a painted surface insulates even on a metal object, and a tarnished/corroded surface or loose clip can give a misleading 'no light'. Choose a dull-metal counter-case where the clip reaches bare metal, and note that bare metal foil conducts, so it is not a valid 'shiny thing that fails' example.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One source (IOP Spark / SPT electric circuits guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; the DfE National Curriculum source is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is carried over as-is and not independently confirmed.

The original assessment offered a 'foil-covered card' as a shiny object that fails to light the bulb; aluminium foil is a conductor and would in fact light it, so this example was replaced with a shiny plastic object or a painted metal tab (paint insulates) as the correct shiny-but-non-conducting counter-case.

The original poeTask/correctAnswer used a 'dull or rusty' metal as the reliable conductor. A heavily rusted or tarnished oxide layer can itself block contact and give a false 'no light', conflicting with the tarnish caveat in the first activity; the counter-case was narrowed to a 'dull/unpolished' metal with a requirement that the clip touch bare metal.

Activity 'Sort and check' carries no sourceClaim because no source claim directly supports the principle that categorisation assesses/consolidates rather than builds investigative reasoning; the DfE claim covers only the topic/outcome.

The original rated dialogue and 3D interactives as 'poor' with reasoning that dialogue 'doesn't develop the test-and-record skill' and that '3D adds cost without conceptual gain'. These are presented here as scope-limited observations (discussion and 3D do not themselves run the empirical test) rather than universal claims; discussion can still support reasoning about results.

The row labels the 2D interactive bench 'ideal' while also noting no digital artefact fully replaces the physical kit; this rewrite foregrounds the physical investigation as the primary activity, consistent with the curriculum framing.

assess.poeTask: Offer a shiny plastic object (or foil-covered card) and a dull or rusty metal object. Ask the child to predict which will light the bulb AND why, before testing each in the circuit. The reason exposes the 'shiny conducts' rule; the dull metal lighting up while the shiny plastic fails violates it. Then test both.
probeDeeper: You found the dull iron conducts. What does that tell you about the 'shiny things conduct' rule?
Why do we put plastic around metal wires — which part does the conducting and which part keeps us safe?
Counterexample: glass is hard and can be shiny, but it doesn't light the bulb. What does that tell you about hardness and shininess as clues?
How could you turn a material you're unsure about into a fair test for conduction?
assess.correctAnswer: What decides it is what the material is made of, not how it looks: metals conduct electricity (let current flow through), while most non-metals such as plastic, wood and rubber are insulators (block it). Shininess doesn't decide it — a shiny plastic still blocks current and a dull metal still conducts. The iron conducts because it's a metal; the ruler blocks it because it's plastic.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shiny or metallic-looking things conduct because they look like metal ('shiny = carries electricity').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test a dull, unpolished metal against a shiny plastic — the outcome flips the surface rule; sort by 'is it actually a metal?'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The shiny material conducts and the dull one doesn't, because shiny things carry electricity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a shiny non-metal (foil-wrapped plastic, shiny painted object) conducts and a dull metal doesn't.

errorPatterns.pattern: The plastic coating on a wire is what carries the electricity ('the wire works because of the plastic').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Strip a wire — the metal inside conducts; the plastic is there to insulate and protect so we aren't shocked.
errorPatterns.distractor: The plastic coating is what carries the electricity along the wire.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the coloured plastic sheath conducts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Anything hard or solid conducts and only soft things insulate ('hard = conductor').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test hard glass and hard wood (insulators) against softer metals — hardness isn't the rule, being a metal is.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Classifies hard wood or glass as conductors.

responseLevels.gap: Classifies by surface cues — shiny/hard/heavy = conductor; thinks the plastic coating conducts.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by material kind (metals conduct, non-metals insulate), dismisses surface cues with a counterexample, and explains that the metal core conducts while the plastic coat insulates for safety.
responseLevels.partial: Knows metals conduct and can classify the tested materials, but still leans on shininess or hardness for unfamiliar ones, or is unsure why wires are coated.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You test a shiny plastic ruler and a dull piece of iron in a circuit. The shiny ruler doesn't let the bulb light, but the dull iron does. Your friend expected the shiny one to conduct because 'shiny things carry electricity.' What actually decides whether a material conducts?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child using surface cues (shiny, hard, heavy = conductor) answers differently from one who classifies by material kind (metal vs non-metal). The reason tier separates 'shiny/hard conducts' from 'metals conduct'.
